extracted.intended_audience: citizens/ratifiers, lawyers, and commentators concerned with the design and interpretation of the federal judiciary under the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative rules for how the federal judiciary's jurisdiction, appeals, and the place of the jury-trial should be understood and arranged under the proposed Constitution. Covers allocation between Supreme, inferior, and state courts and when juries are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate jurisdiction 'both as to law and fact'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution grants the Supreme Court appellate jurisdiction 'both as to law and fact.' This does not necessarily imply a re-examination of facts decided by juries in inferior courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: The Supreme Court 'takes cognizance of [facts] as it appears upon the record, and pronounces the law arising upon it.' The provision was likely meant to permit re-examination in some civil-law style causes (e.g., prize causes) and to be subject to exceptions and regulations by Congress. Scoring/interpretive note: this phrase should be read with reference to the practical need for Congress to qualify appellate fact-review (for example, barring re-examination of jury-tried facts where appropriate) rather than as an absolute abolition of jury determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction of fact and law inseparable in appellate review
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not possible to separate 'fact' and 'law' absolutely; appellate jurisdiction of both means the court examines how facts appear on the record and applies the law arising from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Treat factual findings as they are shown on the record; the appellate court's jurisdiction can embrace fact-as-appearing-on-record even where it does not institute a new factual inquiry. Example: common-law courts having jury fact-finding still 'have jurisdiction of both fact and law' when they render judgment without a jury if facts are agreed in pleadings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional power to regulate appellate review and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution's grant of appellate jurisdiction is subject to 'such exceptions and regulations as the national legislature may prescribe.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: Congress may limit re-examination of facts in appeals (e.g., prevent re-examination of facts originally tried by jury) or qualify appellate jurisdiction (e.g., limit to certain causes). Practical advice: interpret the constitutional grant as enabling legislative modification to 'best answer the ends of public justice and security.'

rubrics_metrics.name: States retain pre-existing authorities unless exclusively delegated
rubrics_metrics.description: State governments keep all previous powers except those exclusively delegated to the federal government: (a) expressly granted exclusively; (b) granted to the Union and prohibited to States; or (c) granted such that state exercise would be incompatible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule of construction: In the absence of explicit exclusion or incompatibility, assume concurrent state jurisdiction. Use this test when deciding whether an authority is taken from a State by implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction of State courts in federal cases unless expressly excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: State courts will generally retain jurisdiction over causes arising under federal law unless they are expressly excluded by the Constitution or subsequent national legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive point: The phrase vesting judicial power in 'one Supreme Court, and in such inferior courts as the Congress shall ... establish' should not be read to exclude state tribunals; appeals are concerned with the objects of appeal, not the particular inferior tribunals from which they come. Practical consequence: appeals should be able to lie from state courts to the Supreme Court to avoid eluding national judiciary authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal subject-matter (objects) governs appellate reach, not originating tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellate jurisdiction is defined by the objects (classes of causes) enumerated, not by limiting appeals to originate only from subordinate federal tribunals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Read 'appellate jurisdiction' terms as extending to state court decisions in the enumerated federal classes; otherwise plaintiffs could elude federal review by choosing state tribunals. Example: to preserve national uniformity, appeals should extend from state courts where federal questions arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional discretion to create inferior courts and define their authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress is authorized to 'constitute tribunals inferior to the Supreme Court' and may determine whether those tribunals exercise original jurisdiction, appellate jurisdiction, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: The legislature can create district courts with appellate authority from state courts, reducing pressure on the Supreme Court and limiting the Supreme Court's appellate docket. Scoring/organizational note: evaluate institutional design proposals with regard to how they use Congress's discretion to balance workloads and preserve state courts' roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence in Constitution does not equal abolition of jury trial in civil cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of an express constitutional provision for trial by jury in civil cases does not imply abolition; silence is not the same as prohibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: The Constitution's express requirement of jury trial in criminal cases does not logically forbid the legislature from providing for civil juries. Interpretive maxim: do not infer negative consequences from mere silence; ask whether the silence arose from impossibility of a common referent (e.g., 'as heretofore' would be meaningless at the federal level).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative power to prescribe mode of trial
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to constitute courts carries with it the power to prescribe modes of trial; hence Congress may decide whether to employ juries in civil causes in federal courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application: Where the Constitution is silent, the legislative branch may adopt jury or non-jury procedures for civil causes; but an express constitutional command (e.g., criminal jury trial) would constrain that discretion. Example: Congress could authoritatively decide that certain civil causes be tried with or without juries depending on policy and local practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of State practices makes a uniform constitutional civil-jury rule impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: Because States vary widely in how and where juries are used (common law, chancery, admiralty, probate differences), a single federal constitutional rule fixing the civil jury's scope would not suit all States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recommendation: Leaving civil jury-regulation to Congress (rather than attempting to constitutionalize 'trial by jury as heretofore') avoids caprice and incoherence across jurisdictions. Evaluate proposals by how well they accommodate existing state heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juries unsuitable for certain categories of causes (prize, admiralty, complex equity)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many cases in which trial by jury is ineligible or inapposite — notably prize causes (laws of nations), admiralty causes, and many equity matters requiring technical, prolonged or policy-sensitive adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification: Juries lack the specialized knowledge and capacity for protracted, minute, or public-policy-sensitive inquiries; use specialized tribunals or bench trials instead. Example: prize causes have historically been tried by special tribunals (e.g., privy council) where facts and law are re-examined to protect international relations; applying juries risks international injury and inconsistent policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of equity and law preserves jury institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining a separation between courts of equity and courts of law helps preserve the jury trial's 'pristine purity'; merging equity into law courts risks undermining the jury system by introducing complex matters unsuited for juries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive/design guidance: Preserve institutional separation where practical; when equity causes require 'long, deliberate, and critical investigation', they should not be committed to juries. Evaluate court-structure proposals by whether they protect the distinct modes of decision-making appropriate to different jurisdictions.
